Hebrew letters, in alphabet order.א Aleph: Aleph is silent, and its name probably means 'ox'. Through Greek alpha it gave us the word 'alphabet'.
Hebrew letters, in alphabet order.ג Gimel: The name is thought to come from the word for camel, and gimel is the ancestor of the Greek gamma and the Latin C and G.
Hebrew letters, in alphabet order.ד Dalet: Meaning 'door', dalet is the ancestor of the Greek delta, a triangular shape like an open tent flap.
Hebrew letters, in alphabet order.ו Vav: Vav, meaning 'hook' or 'nail', also works as a one-letter prefix meaning 'and'.
Hebrew letters, in alphabet order.ז Zayin: Zayin has the numeric value 7, and its shape evolved into the Greek zeta and the Latin Z.
Hebrew letters, in alphabet order.ח Het: Het with yod spells 'chai', meaning life, which adds up to 18, a number that is lucky in Jewish culture.
Hebrew letters, in alphabet order.ל Lamed: Lamed rises above the other letters, making it the tallest in the alphabet. It is the ancestor of the Greek lambda and Latin L.
Hebrew letters, in alphabet order.נ Nun: Nun means 'fish' and is one of five Hebrew letters that change shape at the end of a word.
Hebrew letters, in alphabet order.ע Ayin: Ayin means 'eye', and its original shape was a small circle with a dot, like an eye.
Hebrew letters, in alphabet order.ר Resh: Resh means 'head' and is the ancestor of the Greek rho and the Latin R.

Joyful and Sorrowful Mysteries of the Ro.Annunciation: The Annunciation is the angel Gabriel's announcement to Mary that she will bear Jesus, a scene painted by countless Renaissance artists.
Joyful and Sorrowful Mysteries of the Ro.Visitation: Mary visits her cousin Elizabeth, who is pregnant with John the Baptist, and the scene includes the Magnificat.
Joyful and Sorrowful Mysteries of the Ro.Nativity: The birth of Jesus in Bethlehem, which in tradition happened in a stable because there was no room at the inn.
Joyful and Sorrowful Mysteries of the Ro.Presentation in the Temple: Mary and Joseph bring the infant Jesus to the temple in Jerusalem, where Simeon recognises him as the Messiah.
Joyful and Sorrowful Mysteries of the Ro.Finding in the Temple: At twelve, Jesus is found in the temple talking with teachers after his parents had searched for three days.
Joyful and Sorrowful Mysteries of the Ro.Agony in the Garden: Jesus prays in Gethsemane the night before his death, an olive grove on the Mount of Olives.
Joyful and Sorrowful Mysteries of the Ro.Scourging at the Pillar: Jesus is whipped at a pillar, a moment that appears in the Gospels and in countless works of Christian art.
Joyful and Sorrowful Mysteries of the Ro.Crowning with Thorns: Soldiers mock Jesus by placing a woven crown on his head and dressing him in a purple robe.
Joyful and Sorrowful Mysteries of the Ro.Carrying of the Cross: This follows the road to Golgotha, traditionally marked by the Stations of the Cross in many churches.
Joyful and Sorrowful Mysteries of the Ro.Crucifixion: The final sorrowful mystery is Jesus's death on the cross at Golgotha, central to Christian faith.

Milestones in Earth's long history.Earth forms: Dating of meteorites and the oldest rocks gives the age; the planet grew from dust clumping around the young Sun and was molten early on.
Milestones in Earth's long history.Great Oxidation Event: Cyanobacteria's photosynthesis flooded the air with oxygen, rusting the oceans' dissolved iron and wiping out many oxygen-intolerant microbes.
Milestones in Earth's long history.Snowball Earth: Evidence suggests ice reached near the equator, perhaps more than once. Volcanic carbon dioxide piling up in the air may have finally thawed it.
Milestones in Earth's long history.Cambrian explosion: Most major animal groups show up in the fossil record within a few tens of millions of years, including early creatures with eyes, shells and legs.
Milestones in Earth's long history.First land plants: Small mossy plants without true roots crept ashore, paving the way for soil, forests and, eventually, animals that live on land.
Milestones in Earth's long history.Great Permian extinction: Called the Great Dying, it wiped out roughly 90 percent of marine species and is mainly blamed on enormous volcanic eruptions in Siberia.
Milestones in Earth's long history.First flowering plants: Darwin called their sudden rise an 'abominable mystery'. Flowers recruited insects as pollinators and came to dominate most land habitats.
Milestones in Earth's long history.Dinosaurs wiped out: An asteroid struck near today's Yucatan in Mexico; of the dinosaurs, only the lineage of birds survived.
Milestones in Earth's long history.Himalayas begin rising: India's collision with Asia still pushes the range up a few millimetres a year, and Everest's summit rock is ancient seafloor limestone.
Milestones in Earth's long history.Last Glacial Maximum: Ice sheets kilometres thick covered much of Canada and northern Europe, and sea level was roughly 120 metres lower than it is today.

When these ancient wonders were built.Göbekli Tepe: Its carved stone pillars, raised by hunter-gatherers around 11,500 years ago, predate farming and rewrote ideas about the start of civilization.
When these ancient wonders were built.Great Pyramid of Giza: Built for Khufu, it was the tallest human-made structure on Earth for nearly 4,000 years, and its blocks were fitted with remarkable precision.
When these ancient wonders were built.Ishtar Gate of Babylon: Glazed blue bricks decorated with lions, dragons and bulls made up the gate of Babylon; it was rebuilt inside a Berlin museum.
When these ancient wonders were built.Parthenon: The Athenian temple to Athena sits on the Acropolis and has columns that subtly bulge so they look perfectly straight.
When these ancient wonders were built.Terracotta Army: Thousands of life-size clay soldiers guard the tomb of China's first emperor, and no two faces appear to be identical.
When these ancient wonders were built.Pantheon in Rome: Its concrete dome, still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world, has an open oculus at the top that lets in rain and light.
When these ancient wonders were built.Hagia Sophia: Built as a church under Justinian, it later served as a mosque, a museum, and a mosque again.
When these ancient wonders were built.Borobudur: This huge Buddhist monument in Java, built in layers of stone, lay buried under volcanic ash and jungle for centuries before its rediscovery.
When these ancient wonders were built.Angkor Wat: Originally Hindu, then Buddhist, this Cambodian temple complex is the largest religious monument in the world and appears on the national flag.
When these ancient wonders were built.Machu Picchu: Perched high in the Andes, the Inca estate went unmentioned by the Spanish and became widely known only after Hiram Bingham's 1911 visit.

How much light your eyes deal with.Moonless overcast night: Your eyes rely on rod cells that cannot see colour, and they take about half an hour to fully adapt to darkness.
How much light your eyes deal with.Clear starlit night: Rod cells are so sensitive that under ideal conditions a person can notice a handful of photons.
How much light your eyes deal with.Full moon: A full moon is about a million times dimmer than the sun and reflects only about 12 percent of the light it receives.
How much light your eyes deal with.End of twilight: Astronomers call the deep end of dusk astronomical twilight, when the sky gets dark enough to see faint stars.
How much light your eyes deal with.Living room lamps: Indoor lighting is far dimmer than daytime, which is why stepping outside feels bright, even though your pupils adapt quickly.
How much light your eyes deal with.Very dark overcast day: Even a gloomy storm day outside is about double the light of a typical living room.
How much light your eyes deal with.Office lighting: Standards for offices recommend around 300 to 500 lux, and too little causes eye strain.
How much light your eyes deal with.Overcast day: Clouds block a lot of sunlight, yet an overcast day still delivers about 1,000 lux, roughly one-hundredth of direct sun.
How much light your eyes deal with.Full daylight (shade): Shade is not dark, since skylight alone can supply tens of thousands of lux.
How much light your eyes deal with.Direct sunlight: Direct sun delivers up to about 100,000 lux, which is why phone screens are hard to read outdoors.

James Cameron films by release.Piranha II: The Spawning: Piranha II was Cameron's directorial debut, a low-budget flying-piranha sequel that he later reportedly disowned.
James Cameron films by release.The Terminator: The Terminator was made on a small budget and inspired by a fever dream Cameron had while ill, and it made Arnold Schwarzenegger a star.
James Cameron films by release.Aliens: Aliens turned the horror of Alien into an action-war film, and Sigourney Weaver was nominated for an Oscar for it.
James Cameron films by release.The Abyss: The Abyss pioneered a computer-generated water creature, and the underwater filming took place in a huge abandoned nuclear reactor tank.
James Cameron films by release.Terminator 2: Terminator 2 cost around 100 million dollars, the most expensive film at the time, and won four Oscars for technical categories.
James Cameron films by release.True Lies: True Lies, a spy comedy with Schwarzenegger, was the first film with a budget over 100 million dollars to cross that mark in earnings.
James Cameron films by release.Titanic: Titanic won 11 Oscars, and Cameron dived to the actual wreck multiple times, including during research for the film.
James Cameron films by release.Avatar: Avatar became the highest-grossing film ever, and it pioneered 3D filming and performance-capture.
James Cameron films by release.Avatar: The Way of Water: The Way of Water took 13 years to follow the first film and featured actors learning to hold their breath for minutes for underwater scenes.
James Cameron films by release.Avatar: Fire and Ash: Fire and Ash is the third Avatar film, and introduces a more aggressive Na'vi clan, the Ash People.

When these cities were founded.Carthage: Legend says Queen Dido founded it, and it later became Rome's great rival in the Punic Wars.
When these cities were founded.Rome: Tradition says Romulus founded it after killing his brother Remus, and Romans counted years from this date.
When these cities were founded.Byzantium: Greek colonists led by Byzas founded it, and it later became Constantinople and then Istanbul.
When these cities were founded.Massalia (Marseille): Greek settlers from Phocaea founded it, which makes Marseille France's oldest city.
When these cities were founded.Alexandria: Alexander the Great founded it, and it later housed the Pharos lighthouse and the Great Library.
When these cities were founded.Lugdunum (Lyon): The capital of Roman Gaul was Lyon today, and the emperor Claudius was born there.
When these cities were founded.Baghdad: Caliph al-Mansur built a round city here, which became home to the House of Wisdom.
When these cities were founded.Heian-kyō (Kyoto): Modelled on the Chinese capital Chang'an, it served as Japan's capital for over a thousand years.
When these cities were founded.Cairo: The Fatimid dynasty founded it as al-Qahira, 'the victorious', and the al-Azhar mosque followed in 970.
When these cities were founded.Tenochtitlan: The Aztec capital stood on an island in Lake Texcoco, with canals and causeways, and later became Mexico City.

How many people each of these can carry.Wright Flyer: The pilot lay face-down on the lower wing, shifting his hips in a cradle that warped the wings to steer.
How many people each of these can carry.Apollo spacecraft: Apollo 13's three crew survived in a lunar module designed for two after an oxygen tank failed.
How many people each of these can carry.Space Shuttle: It flew 135 missions between 1981 and 2011, and in 1985 once crammed eight crew aboard.
How many people each of these can carry.Routemaster bus (seated): The iconic London double-decker, introduced in 1956, with an open rear platform that let passengers hop on and off.
How many people each of these can carry.Concorde: It crossed the Atlantic in about three and a half hours at twice the speed of sound, and its cabin was famously narrow.
How many people each of these can carry.Boeing 737-800 (max): Its engines are flattened on the bottom to fit beneath the low wing, giving the 737 a recognizable look.
How many people each of these can carry.Airbus A380 (max): Some airlines fitted onboard showers, though the 853 figure is the certified all-economy maximum; typical layouts seat about 500.
How many people each of these can carry.16-car N700 Shinkansen: These Japanese bullet trains are famously punctual, with average delays measured in about a minute a year.
How many people each of these can carry.RMS Titanic (all aboard): Lifeboats seated only about 1,178 people, around a third of those aboard.
How many people each of these can carry.Icon of the Seas (max guests): When launched in 2024, it became the largest cruise ship in the world, with eight neighborhoods and a huge waterpark.

Pre-decimal British money.Farthing: Its name comes from 'fourthing', a quarter of a penny; the coin showed a tiny wren, Britain's smallest bird, and was withdrawn in 1961.
Pre-decimal British money.Penny: The abbreviation d comes from denarius, the Roman coin, and Britain kept writing pence that way until decimalisation in 1971.
Pre-decimal British money.Threepence: Pronounced 'thruppence', the twelve-sided brass version introduced in 1937 stayed in circulation until decimalisation in 1971.
Pre-decimal British money.Sixpence: Nicknamed the tanner, this is the coin traditionally baked into Christmas puddings, and a silver sixpence in a bride's shoe was said to bring luck.
Pre-decimal British money.Shilling: Twelve pence made a shilling and twenty shillings made a pound; the slang 'bob' lived on in the Scouts' 'bob a job' fundraising weeks.
Pre-decimal British money.Florin: Introduced in 1849 as a tenth of a pound, the two-shilling florin was a first step toward decimal money, named after Florence's gold coin.
Pre-decimal British money.Half crown: Worth two shillings and sixpence, an eighth of a pound, this large coin was withdrawn shortly before decimalisation in 1971.
Pre-decimal British money.Crown: Five shillings, a quarter of a pound; by the 20th century crowns were mostly commemorative, like the 1965 coin for Winston Churchill.
Pre-decimal British money.Pound: A pound was 240 pence because it once meant a pound weight of silver pennies, and the symbol £ comes from the Latin libra.
Pre-decimal British money.Guinea: Worth 21 shillings, it was named for the West African gold it was first minted from; horse sales and art auctions still price in guineas.

When these dairy brands were founded.Kraft: James L. Kraft started by selling cheese from a horse-drawn wagon in Chicago and patented processed cheese in 1916.
When these dairy brands were founded.Tillamook: A farmer-owned co-op on Oregon's coast, it is best known for its cheddar, and is named after the county.
When these dairy brands were founded.Danone: Isaac Carasso started making yogurt in Barcelona, and named it for his son Daniel, nicknamed 'Danon', or little Daniel in Catalan.
When these dairy brands were founded.Land O'Lakes: Based in Minnesota, its butter box once carried a Native American maiden, a logo retired in 2020.
When these dairy brands were founded.Fage: This Greek family company's strained yogurt, pronounced 'fa-yeh', introduced thick Greek yogurt to many American and British shoppers.
When these dairy brands were founded.Babybel: This little round cheese in its red wax coat is made by the French company Bel, and the wax can be reused as a modelling material.
When these dairy brands were founded.Kerrygold: Created by the Irish Dairy Board, its butter's golden colour comes from grass-fed cows on pasture.
When these dairy brands were founded.Yoplait: The name blends two co-operatives, 'Yo' from yogurt and 'Plait' from Coplait, in a joining of French dairies.
When these dairy brands were founded.Activia: A Danone yogurt marketed for digestion with a probiotic bacterium; its health claims led to legal settlements in the United States.
When these dairy brands were founded.Chobani: Turkish immigrant Hamdi Ulukaya bought a closed Kraft yogurt plant in upstate New York for it, and sold the first tubs in 2007.

When these African nations became indepe.Liberia: Founded by freed African Americans, its capital Monrovia is named for US president James Monroe.
When these African nations became indepe.Egypt: Britain declared it sovereign, though British troops remained for years.
When these African nations became indepe.Libya: It was the first African nation to gain independence through the United Nations.
When these African nations became indepe.Sudan: For decades it was Africa's largest country by area until South Sudan split off.
When these African nations became indepe.Kenya: Jomo Kenyatta became its first leader after the Mau Mau uprising.
When these African nations became indepe.Angola: Independence from Portugal followed the Carnation Revolution, and civil war began soon after.
When these African nations became indepe.Zimbabwe: Robert Mugabe led it from independence until 2017.
When these African nations became indepe.Namibia: It ended decades of South African rule over it, after a long struggle.
When these African nations became indepe.Eritrea: It gained independence after a 30-year war and a referendum.
When these African nations became indepe.South Sudan: It is the world's newest recognized country, and it split from Sudan after a referendum.

When these gold rushes began.Minas Gerais, Brazil: Brazil's rush made Portugal rich and drew hundreds of thousands of settlers; the name of the region means general mines.
When these gold rushes began.California: James Marshall's find at Sutter's Mill drew some 300,000 forty-niners and turned San Francisco from a village into a city.
When these gold rushes began.Victoria, Australia: Ballarat and Bendigo's diggings multiplied the colony's population within a decade, and the Eureka Stockade rebellion followed in 1854.
When these gold rushes began.Fraser Canyon, Canada: Miners from California flooded in, and the rush led Britain to create the colony of British Columbia in 1858.
When these gold rushes began.Otago, New Zealand: The strike at Gabriel's Gully made Dunedin New Zealand's largest city for a time.
When these gold rushes began.Black Hills: Gold found on land guaranteed to the Lakota by treaty helped spark the Great Sioux War, which included the Battle of Little Bighorn.
When these gold rushes began.Witwatersrand: The Witwatersrand reef is the richest gold deposit ever found, and Johannesburg grew out of the rush.
When these gold rushes began.Kalgoorlie: Paddy Hannan's find started it, and the nearby Super Pit is still one of Australia's largest open-cut gold mines.
When these gold rushes began.Klondike: Around 100,000 set out, perhaps 30,000 reached Dawson City, and few got rich, though Jack London and Robert Service wrote about it.
When these gold rushes began.Nome, Alaska: Gold was found in the beach sand itself, and miners panned the shoreline; Nome briefly became Alaska's biggest town.

Books with a color in the title, by year.The Red and the Black: Stendhal's novel follows ambitious Julien Sorel; the title colors are often read as the army and the clergy, two paths to rise in society.
Books with a color in the title, by year.The Scarlet Letter: Hawthorne's tale of Hester Prynne and her forced red A is set in Puritan Boston; he descended from a judge of the Salem witch trials.
Books with a color in the title, by year.The Woman in White: Wilkie Collins's serialized hit was a pioneering sensation novel and an ancestor of detective fiction, run in Dickens's magazine.
Books with a color in the title, by year.Black Beauty: Narrated by a horse, it was Anna Sewell's only novel and helped fuel reforms against cruelties such as tight bearing reins.
Books with a color in the title, by year.A Study in Scarlet: It introduced Sherlock Holmes and Dr Watson to the world, and Arthur Conan Doyle was paid just 25 pounds for it.
Books with a color in the title, by year.The Red Badge of Courage: Stephen Crane wrote this Civil War novel without having seen combat, and it made him famous at just 24.
Books with a color in the title, by year.Anne of Green Gables: L. M. Montgomery's red-haired orphan lives on Prince Edward Island, and the book sold millions and spawned many sequels.
Books with a color in the title, by year.A Clockwork Orange: Anthony Burgess invented the teen slang Nadsat, a blend of Russian and English, and Kubrick's 1971 film made the book notorious.
Books with a color in the title, by year.The Bluest Eye: Toni Morrison's first novel follows Pecola, a Black girl who longs for blue eyes; Morrison would win the Nobel Prize in 1993.
Books with a color in the title, by year.The Color Purple: Alice Walker's novel told in letters won the Pulitzer Prize in 1983, making her the first Black woman to win it for fiction.

British note names by length.Hemidemisemiquaver: In US terms this is a 64th note, which makes its British name a tongue twister.
British note names by length.Demisemiquaver: The name stacks prefixes: semi means half, demi half again; Americans call it a 32nd note.
British note names by length.Semiquaver: In the US it's a sixteenth note; two flags on its stem mark it, and 'semi' means half a quaver.
British note names by length.Quaver: Its name comes from the verb 'to quaver', to tremble; Americans call it an eighth note.
British note names by length.Crotchet: The name comes from French for 'little hook' and from the shape of its original notation; the US calls it a quarter note.
British note names by length.Dotted crotchet: The dot lengthens a note by half, so this is a crotchet joined to a quaver, a pattern at the heart of many jigs.
British note names by length.Minim: The word means 'smallest', because in medieval music it was the shortest note; today it's a half note.
British note names by length.Dotted minim: Three beats fill a whole bar in waltz time, which is why it's the note to hold for a bar of 3/4.
British note names by length.Semibreve: Its name means 'half a breve'; in the US it's a whole note, drawn as an open oval without a stem.
British note names by length.Breve: The name means 'short', since in medieval notation it was a brief note; now it's the longest in common use, called a double whole note in the US.

Native Japanese counting words, by value.hitotsu: One. This native series counts objects up to ten, as in one apple. The same root appears in hitori, the word for one person.
Native Japanese counting words, by value.futatsu: Two. Alongside the Chinese-derived numbers, this older Japanese set is still used for counting everyday objects and the ages of small children.
Native Japanese counting words, by value.mittsu: Three. The "mitsu" root appears in the company name Mitsubishi, which means "three water chestnuts", describing its diamond-like logo.
Native Japanese counting words, by value.yottsu: Four. Japanese often avoids the Chinese-derived "shi" for four because it sounds like the word for death, so "yon" and "yottsu" are preferred.
Native Japanese counting words, by value.itsutsu: Five. Japan's Shichi-Go-San festival celebrates children at ages three, five and seven, with families visiting shrines in November.
Native Japanese counting words, by value.muttsu: Six. The native series stops at ten, so for eleven and above Japanese switches to Chinese-derived numbers, as in "juu-ichi".
Native Japanese counting words, by value.nanatsu: Seven. "Nanatsu no Taizai", the manga known in English as The Seven Deadly Sins, uses this word in its title.
Native Japanese counting words, by value.yattsu: Eight. The character for eight widens as it goes downward, and the Japanese see this spreading shape, "suehirogari", as lucky.
Native Japanese counting words, by value.kokonotsu: Nine. The Chinese-derived "ku" sounds like the word for suffering, so Japanese often prefers the "kyuu" reading or this native word instead.
Native Japanese counting words, by value.tō: Ten. The only word in the series that does not end in "-tsu", and it is also the cutoff after which counting switches to the Chinese-derived words.

Cold temperatures, from absolute zero up.Absolute zero: The point where particles have minimal motion; scientists have cooled atoms to billionths of a degree above it.
Cold temperatures, from absolute zero up.Liquid helium: Helium stays liquid down to absolute zero at normal pressure, and near -271 °C it becomes a superfluid that flows without friction.
Cold temperatures, from absolute zero up.Liquid nitrogen: This liquid boils at -196 °C and is used for freezing warts and preserving biological samples.
Cold temperatures, from absolute zero up.Liquid oxygen: Liquid oxygen is pale blue, and it clings to a magnet because oxygen is paramagnetic.
Cold temperatures, from absolute zero up.Coldest air on Earth (Vostok): The Russian base's 1983 reading is still the lowest air temperature reliably measured on Earth.
Cold temperatures, from absolute zero up.Dry ice: Solid carbon dioxide skips the liquid phase and turns straight to gas, which is why it makes fog effects.
Cold temperatures, from absolute zero up.Mercury freezes: This is the only common metal that's liquid at room temperature, and it freezes at about -39 °C.
Cold temperatures, from absolute zero up.Home freezer: A typical freezer is set to this temperature, cold enough to stop food-spoiling bacteria from growing.
Cold temperatures, from absolute zero up.Water freezes: Pure water can stay liquid several degrees below this if it's very still, a state called supercooling.
Cold temperatures, from absolute zero up.Fridge: Fridges are set to about 4 °C because bacteria slow down greatly below 5 °C.

When these TV cooking shows premiered.The French Chef: Julia Child's Boston-made show turned her into a star; she shrugged off kitchen mishaps on camera, which won viewers over.
When these TV cooking shows premiered.The Galloping Gourmet: Host Graham Kerr, a flamboyant Briton, opened shows by leaping over a chair, glass of wine in hand, before cooking lavish dishes.
When these TV cooking shows premiered.Yan Can Cook: Martin Yan's catchphrase was 'If Yan can cook, so can you!', and his quick cleaver work made Chinese cooking look easy.
When these TV cooking shows premiered.Iron Chef: This Japanese show staged cook-offs in 'Kitchen Stadium' around a secret ingredient, and inspired American and other versions.
When these TV cooking shows premiered.Two Fat Ladies: Jennifer Paterson and Clarissa Dickson Wright crossed Britain by motorbike and sidecar, cooking with plenty of butter and cream.
When these TV cooking shows premiered.The Naked Chef: Jamie Oliver's 'naked' meant stripped-down, simple food, not the chef; the show made him a star in Britain.
When these TV cooking shows premiered.Kitchen Nightmares (UK): Gordon Ramsay's British original, on Channel 4, sent him into struggling restaurants before the show was remade in America.
When these TV cooking shows premiered.Top Chef: Bravo's contest has been hosted by Padma Lakshmi for most of its run, and sends winners off with a title and prize money.
When these TV cooking shows premiered.Chopped: Contestants open mystery baskets and must turn odd ingredients into appetizer, entree and dessert, losing a chef each round.
When these TV cooking shows premiered.Nailed It!: This Netflix show, hosted by Nicole Byer, invites amateur bakers to recreate stunning cakes, with gloriously wonky results.

Summer Olympic host cities from north to.Helsinki: It was awarded the 1940 Games, which war cancelled, and finally hosted in 1952. Its stadium tower is still a city landmark.
Summer Olympic host cities from north to.Moscow: The 1980 Games were boycotted by the United States and dozens of other nations over the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan.
Summer Olympic host cities from north to.London: The only city to host the modern Summer Games three times: 1908, 1948 and 2012.
Summer Olympic host cities from north to.Paris: It hosted in 1900, 1924 and 2024, and the 1924 Games inspired the film Chariots of Fire.
Summer Olympic host cities from north to.Montreal: Its 1976 stadium was nicknamed 'the Big Owe', as the debt for the Games took about three decades to pay off.
Summer Olympic host cities from north to.Barcelona: The 1992 Games reopened the city to the sea, as old industrial waterfront was turned into beaches and a marina.
Summer Olympic host cities from north to.Atlanta: The 1996 Games marked the centennial of the modern Olympics, in the home city of Coca-Cola.
Summer Olympic host cities from north to.Mexico City: At roughly 2,240 metres up, its 1968 Games thin air helped Bob Beamon leap 8.90 metres, a long jump record that stood for 23 years.
Summer Olympic host cities from north to.Rio de Janeiro: In 2016 it became the first South American city to host the Summer Games.
Summer Olympic host cities from north to.Melbourne: In 1956 it hosted the first Games in the southern hemisphere. Horse events were held in Stockholm because of Australian quarantine rules.

Famous stars by distance from Earth.Proxima Centauri: The closest star to the Sun is a small red dwarf, and it hosts at least one planet in its habitable zone.
Famous stars by distance from Earth.Barnard's Star: This red dwarf moves faster across our sky than any other star, and it has the highest proper motion.
Famous stars by distance from Earth.Sirius: The brightest star in the night sky has a faint white dwarf companion nicknamed the Pup, and it was seen by ancient Egyptians.
Famous stars by distance from Earth.Procyon: Its name means 'before the dog', as it rises before Sirius, and it is a binary star with a white dwarf.
Famous stars by distance from Earth.Altair: It spins so fast that it takes only about nine hours to rotate, and it is flattened at the poles.
Famous stars by distance from Earth.Vega: This star was once the north star, and it is the second brightest star in the northern sky, and it was the first to be photographed.
Famous stars by distance from Earth.Arcturus: The brightest star in the northern hemisphere is an orange giant, and it appears in the constellation Boötes.
Famous stars by distance from Earth.Aldebaran: The red giant is the eye of Taurus the bull, and the name comes from the Arabic for 'the follower'.
Famous stars by distance from Earth.Rigel: This blue supergiant forms one foot of Orion, and its brightness is around 120,000 times that of the Sun.
Famous stars by distance from Earth.Deneb: This distant supergiant in Cygnus is one of the most luminous stars visible to the naked eye, and it forms the Northern Cross.

Famous volcanic eruptions, in order.Thera (Santorini), Minoan: One of the largest eruptions in human history, it may have contributed to the decline of Minoan civilization.
Famous volcanic eruptions, in order.Vesuvius buries Pompeii: It buried Pompeii and Herculaneum, and Pliny the Younger described it in letters.
Famous volcanic eruptions, in order.Tambora: In Indonesia, it was followed by 1816, the year without a summer, when crops failed across the Northern Hemisphere.
Famous volcanic eruptions, in order.Krakatoa: Heard about 4,800 km away, it was one of the loudest sounds ever recorded.
Famous volcanic eruptions, in order.Mount Pelée: It wiped out Saint-Pierre on Martinique, killing nearly 30,000, and a prisoner in a dungeon cell survived.
Famous volcanic eruptions, in order.Mount St. Helens: The north flank collapsed in Washington state, and the blast killed 57 people.
Famous volcanic eruptions, in order.Nevado del Ruiz: Lahars buried the town of Armero in Colombia, killing about 23,000.
Famous volcanic eruptions, in order.Pinatubo: The Philippine eruption cooled the global climate by about half a degree for a year or two.
Famous volcanic eruptions, in order.Eyjafjallajökull: Ash grounded flights across Europe for days, and the name is famously hard to pronounce.
Famous volcanic eruptions, in order.Hunga Tonga: The underwater eruption sent a shock wave around the globe several times.

Time spans in plain days.10,000 seconds: That is about the length of a long film, and well under half a working day.
Time spans in plain days.1,000 minutes: Almost a day, but not quite; a Martian day, or sol, lasts about 24 hours and 40 minutes.
Time spans in plain days.100 hours: Apollo 11 took about 76 hours to reach lunar orbit, which is not much shorter than this span.
Time spans in plain days.1 million seconds: A million seconds is under 12 days, while a billion is over 31 years, a gap people tend to underestimate.
Time spans in plain days.100,000 minutes: It is shorter than a Mercury year of 88 days, the length of its orbit around the Sun.
Time spans in plain days.10,000 hours: The 10,000-hour rule popularised by Malcolm Gladwell came from a study of violinists, and the researcher disputed the simplification.
Time spans in plain days.1 million minutes: It is close to a Martian year, which lasts about 687 Earth days.
Time spans in plain days.1,000 days: John F. Kennedy's presidency is known as the thousand days, though it lasted a little longer.
Time spans in plain days.1 billion seconds: A billion seconds ago, you were an adult in the world of three decades back, before the web existed.
Time spans in plain days.1 trillion seconds: A trillion seconds ago, Neanderthals had just vanished and cave art was young.

Women's milestones in space.Valentina Tereshkova flies: She orbited 48 times in almost three days, and remains the only woman to have flown a solo space mission.
Women's milestones in space.Sally Ride flies: Aged 32, the Challenger astronaut became the youngest American in space.
Women's milestones in space.Savitskaya's spacewalk: She walked in space for about 3.5 hours outside Salyut 7, cutting and welding metal.
Women's milestones in space.Helen Sharman, first Briton: A chemist who answered a radio ad, she flew to Mir as Britain's first astronaut.
Women's milestones in space.Mae Jemison flies: A doctor and the first Black woman in space, she later appeared in Star Trek: The Next Generation.
Women's milestones in space.Eileen Collins pilots Shuttle: Eileen Collins became the first woman to pilot a Space Shuttle, flying Discovery.
Women's milestones in space.Collins commands Shuttle: She commanded Columbia on STS-93, which launched the Chandra X-ray Observatory.
Women's milestones in space.Peggy Whitson commands ISS: She has commanded the station twice and holds the US record for total time in space, over 600 days.
Women's milestones in space.Liu Yang, first Chinese woman: She flew aboard Shenzhou 9 to China's Tiangong-1 space lab.
Women's milestones in space.First all-female spacewalk: Christina Koch and Jessica Meir stepped out in October 2019 to swap a failed power controller.

Machines beating humans at games.Nimatron plays Nim: Built for the 1940 New York World's Fair, this machine played the game of Nim and won the great majority of its games against visitors.
Machines beating humans at games.Turochamp chess program: Alan Turing and David Champernowne wrote it, but no computer could run it, so Turing worked out its moves by hand on paper.
Machines beating humans at games.TD-Gammon: Gerald Tesauro's program taught itself backgammon by playing against itself, and it reached near-expert human level.
Machines beating humans at games.Chinook (checkers): Built at the University of Alberta, it took the checkers title in 1994 when champion Marion Tinsley withdrew ill. Checkers was fully solved in 2007.
Machines beating humans at games.Deep Blue beats Kasparov: IBM's machine beat world champion Garry Kasparov 3.5 to 2.5, the first time a computer beat a reigning champion in a match.
Machines beating humans at games.Watson wins Jeopardy!: IBM's system won against the best-ever human champions Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter, answering clues phrased in natural language.
Machines beating humans at games.AlphaGo beats Lee Sedol: Beat Lee Sedol 4 to 1 at Go, a game with more possible positions than atoms in the observable universe. Its odd 'move 37' stunned experts.
Machines beating humans at games.Libratus wins at poker: Carnegie Mellon's AI beat four top professionals in a 20-day heads-up no-limit Texas hold'em match, a game of hidden information.
Machines beating humans at games.AlphaStar (StarCraft II): DeepMind's agent reached Grandmaster level in StarCraft II, ranking above about 99.8 percent of players while limited to human-like controls.
Machines beating humans at games.Cicero plays Diplomacy: Meta's AI negotiated in plain English with real players in Diplomacy, a game built on alliances and betrayal, and scored in the top tenth.

How many founding members these alliance.Triple Alliance: Italy switched sides in World War I, joining the Allies in 1915.
How many founding members these alliance.Mercosur: Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay founded this South American bloc in 1991; the name means 'Southern Common Market'.
How many founding members these alliance.ASEAN: Founded in Bangkok in 1967 by five nations, it now has ten members.
How many founding members these alliance.European Economic Community: France, West Germany, Italy and the Benelux nations formed it in the 1957 Treaty of Rome, and it grew into the EU.
How many founding members these alliance.Warsaw Pact: It was the Soviet-led answer to NATO, formed in 1955 and dissolved in 1991.
How many founding members these alliance.NATO: Article 5 of its 1949 charter says an attack on one is an attack on all, and it has been invoked once, after 9/11.
How many founding members these alliance.Non-Aligned Movement: Founded in Belgrade in 1961, it aimed to stay out of the Cold War blocs, led by Tito, Nehru and Nasser.
How many founding members these alliance.Org. of African Unity: Founded in Addis Ababa in 1963, it was replaced by the African Union in 2002.
How many founding members these alliance.League of Nations: Proposed by Woodrow Wilson, it never included the US and failed to prevent World War II.
How many founding members these alliance.United Nations: Fifty-one countries signed its charter in San Francisco in 1945; it now has 193 members.

Candy-making: the stages of cooking suga.Simmering water: Water just under a simmer is the gentle heat used in poaching, where tiny bubbles barely break the surface.
Candy-making: the stages of cooking suga.Water boils: At sea level water boils at 100°C, though high altitude lowers that temperature, which is why mountain-top cooking takes longer.
Candy-making: the stages of cooking suga.Thread stage: At thread stage a drop of syrup forms a thin thread when pulled between your fingers, the stage used for syrups and some glazes.
Candy-making: the stages of cooking suga.Soft-ball stage: At this stage a drop in cold water forms a soft ball that flattens in your fingers; it's the stage used for fudge and fondant.
Candy-making: the stages of cooking suga.Firm-ball stage: Firm-ball syrup holds its shape yet squishes when pressed, and it's the stage used to make caramels.
Candy-making: the stages of cooking suga.Hard-ball stage: At hard-ball stage, sugar sets firm but still bends slightly, perfect for nougat and marshmallows.
Candy-making: the stages of cooking suga.Soft-crack stage: At soft-crack stage syrup separates into hard but slightly bendy threads, which is used for taffy and butterscotch.
Candy-making: the stages of cooking suga.Hard-crack stage: At hard-crack stage a drop snaps and shatters in cold water, the stage used for lollipops and brittle.
Candy-making: the stages of cooking suga.Caramel: Sugar begins turning into caramel as it browns, producing hundreds of new flavor compounds, from nutty to bittersweet.
Candy-making: the stages of cooking suga.Burnt sugar (black jack): Sugar this hot, sometimes called black jack, is burnt and bitter, though the dark color is traditionally used to tint gravies and cakes.

Top speeds of animals (and one human).Garden snail: Though it eats and moves at a snail's pace, it travels on a single muscular foot, riding ripples along a film of slime.
Top speeds of animals (and one human).Three-toed sloth: It moves so slowly that algae grows on its fur, and it descends from the trees only about once a week to relieve itself.
Top speeds of animals (and one human).Chicken: Chickens descend from red junglefowl of Southeast Asia, and the longest recorded chicken flight lasted 13 seconds.
Top speeds of animals (and one human).Hippopotamus: Despite weighing over a tonne, it can outrun a person in a short sprint, and spends most days submerged.
Top speeds of animals (and one human).Usain Bolt: Usain Bolt's top speed came during his 9.58-second 100 m world record in Berlin in 2009.
Top speeds of animals (and one human).Grizzly bear: Despite weighing hundreds of kilograms, it can sprint at this speed for short distances.
Top speeds of animals (and one human).Ostrich: The largest living bird is also the fastest on land, and its two-toed feet make it a runner, not a flyer.
Top speeds of animals (and one human).Pronghorn: It is the fastest land animal in North America, and can keep a high speed up far longer than a cheetah can.
Top speeds of animals (and one human).Cheetah: It can accelerate to 100 km/h in about three seconds, but tires after a sprint of just 20 or 30 seconds.
Top speeds of animals (and one human).Peregrine falcon (dive): The peregrine's stoop is the fastest speed of any animal, and small bony cones in its nostrils help it breathe while diving.

When these famous sieges took place.Troy (traditional date): The siege of Troy is traditionally dated to around 1184 BC, but archaeologists still debate how much of Homer's tale is true.
When these famous sieges took place.Lachish: Assyria's King Sennacherib besieged Lachish, and he carved a vivid relief of the battle for his palace at Nineveh.
When these famous sieges took place.Tyre: Alexander the Great took Tyre by building a causeway out to the island city, which turned the island into a peninsula.
When these famous sieges took place.Syracuse: Syracuse held out for two years against Rome, while Archimedes' war machines reportedly helped defend it.
When these famous sieges took place.Alesia: Caesar trapped the Gallic leader Vercingetorix in Alesia, and built double walls, one to hold him in and one to keep reinforcements out.
When these famous sieges took place.Masada: At Masada, a desert fortress, Jewish rebels reportedly chose death over capture by the Romans, after a long siege ramp was built.
When these famous sieges took place.Paris, by the Vikings: The Vikings besieged Paris for around a year, and the city survived, though the king paid them a heavy ransom.
When these famous sieges took place.Jerusalem, First Crusade: Crusaders took Jerusalem after a siege of about five weeks, setting up the Kingdom of Jerusalem.
When these famous sieges took place.Orléans: Joan of Arc relieved Orleans, turning the tide for France in the Hundred Years' War when she was only about 17.
When these famous sieges took place.Constantinople, by Mehmed II: Mehmed II's army used massive cannons to breach Constantinople's walls, ending the Byzantine Empire after about 1,000 years.

When these TV channels and services laun.BBC Television: The world's first regular public high-definition TV service launched from Alexandra Palace in London.
When these TV channels and services laun.ITV: Britain's first commercial channel. Its first advertisement was for Gibbs SR toothpaste.
When these TV channels and services laun.HBO: Home Box Office started as a pay service, with its first broadcast a hockey game and a movie.
When these TV channels and services laun.CNN: The first 24-hour news channel, launched by Ted Turner with anchors Bernard Shaw and Lois Hart.
When these TV channels and services laun.MTV: It launched with 'Video Killed the Radio Star' by The Buggles.
When these TV channels and services laun.Disney Channel: Started as a premium subscription service, only turning into a basic cable channel in 1997.
When these TV channels and services laun.Fox (network): Rupert Murdoch's network, launched with The Late Show starring Joan Rivers, hit its stride with The Simpsons.
When these TV channels and services laun.Cartoon Network: Drawing on the Hanna-Barbera library, it later launched hits like Dexter's Laboratory from the 'What a Cartoon!' showcase.
When these TV channels and services laun.Netflix streaming: It began as a DVD-by-mail service in 1997 and began streaming a decade later.
When these TV channels and services laun.Disney+: It gained over ten million subscribers on its first day.

How tall these monuments are.Manneken Pis: Brussels' tiny bronze boy owns a wardrobe of over a thousand costumes, and he is dressed up on special occasions.
How tall these monuments are.The Little Mermaid: Copenhagen's statue honors Hans Christian Andersen's fairy tale; brewer Carl Jacobsen commissioned it after seeing a ballet of the story.
How tall these monuments are.Angel of the North: Antony Gormley's rust-colored steel angel near Gateshead has wings 54 m across, nearly as wide as a jumbo jet's.
How tall these monuments are.Christ the Redeemer: Rio's Art Deco statue was finished in 1931, is clad in small soapstone tiles, and is struck by lightning several times a year.
How tall these monuments are.Arc de Triomphe: Napoleon ordered it in 1806 to honor his armies, but it was finished only in 1836; the Unknown Soldier now lies beneath it.
How tall these monuments are.Leaning Tower of Pisa: Soft ground began tilting it while it was still being built in the 12th century; modern engineers have reduced the lean.
How tall these monuments are.The Motherland Calls: Overlooking Volgograd, it honors the Battle of Stalingrad; the sword alone is about 33 m long, and the statue is mostly concrete.
How tall these monuments are.Elizabeth Tower (Big Ben): Strictly, Big Ben is the great bell inside; the tower itself was renamed for Elizabeth II's Diamond Jubilee in 2012.
How tall these monuments are.Washington Monument: Construction paused for years, so the stone changes shade partway up; at completion in 1884 it was the world's tallest structure.
How tall these monuments are.Gateway Arch, St. Louis: Eero Saarinen's stainless-steel arch is exactly as wide at its base as it is tall, and a small tram carries visitors up inside.

Japan's natural disasters, in order.Mount Fuji's Hōei eruption: Fuji's last eruption, in 1707, rained ash over Edo (now Tokyo), about 100 km away, and the mountain has been quiet ever since.
Japan's natural disasters, in order.Unzen collapse and tsunami: A volcanic dome at Mount Unzen collapsed and triggered a tsunami across the Ariake Sea; about 15,000 died, Japan's deadliest volcanic disaster.
Japan's natural disasters, in order.Ansei Tōkai earthquake: It struck a day before the Ansei Nankai quake; its tsunami wrecked the Russian frigate Diana, which was visiting Shimoda.
Japan's natural disasters, in order.Great Kantō earthquake: Tokyo and Yokohama were devastated, mostly by fire; every 1 September, Japan marks Disaster Prevention Day in remembrance.
Japan's natural disasters, in order.Typhoon Vera (Isewan): One of Japan's deadliest typhoons, it flooded Ise Bay and killed over 5,000 people, and led to the 1961 Disaster Countermeasures Basic Act.
Japan's natural disasters, in order.Kobe earthquake: The Great Hanshin earthquake killed over 6,000 and sparked a surge of volunteering so large that 1995 is called Japan's 'volunteer first year'.
Japan's natural disasters, in order.Tōhoku earthquake: At magnitude 9.0 it is the strongest quake ever recorded in Japan; its tsunami triggered the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear accident.
Japan's natural disasters, in order.Mount Ontake eruption: A sudden steam-driven blast hit around midday while climbers were near the summit, killing 63 in Japan's deadliest eruption since the war.
Japan's natural disasters, in order.Kumamoto earthquakes: Two powerful quakes, a magnitude 6.2 foreshock and a 7.0 mainshock, struck within about 28 hours and damaged Kumamoto Castle.
Japan's natural disasters, in order.Noto Peninsula earthquake: A magnitude 7.5 quake struck on New Year's Day and lifted parts of the Noto coastline by several metres, stranding harbours above the sea.

Deserts by area.Namib Desert: Often called the oldest desert on Earth, it stretches along Namibia's coast. Fog from the Atlantic gives some desert animals their only water.
Deserts by area.Mojave Desert: This US desert holds Death Valley, which recorded the hottest air temperature ever measured on Earth, 56.7 degrees Celsius, in 1913. It also has the Joshua trees.
Deserts by area.Thar Desert: Also called the Great Indian Desert, it covers parts of India and Pakistan. Despite its dryness, it is among the most densely populated deserts in the world.
Deserts by area.Great Victoria Desert: Australia's largest desert is a patchwork of sand dunes and plains in the south of the continent. It is sparsely populated and mostly remote.
Deserts by area.Patagonian Desert: The biggest desert in Argentina lies east of the Andes, in the rain shadow of the mountains. It is cold, windy and rich in fossils.
Deserts by area.Kalahari: It is a semi-desert covering much of Botswana and neighbouring countries. It is home to meerkats, and to the San people, who have lived there for millennia.
Deserts by area.Gobi: This cold desert spans parts of Mongolia and China. In 1920s expeditions, scientists found the first known dinosaur eggs here.
Deserts by area.Arabian Desert: Home to the Rub' al Khali, or Empty Quarter, the largest continuous sand desert in the world. Camels have been central to desert life here for millennia.
Deserts by area.Sahara: The largest hot desert in the world is about the size of the United States. Thousands of years ago, it was green, with grasslands and lakes.
Deserts by area.Antarctic Desert: Antarctica counts as a desert because it gets very little precipitation, and some valleys there have had no rain for millions of years.

The Three Little Pigs, in story order.The pigs leave home: The English tale was printed by James Halliwell in the 1840s, though it was told aloud much longer.
The Three Little Pigs, in story order.Wolf knocks at the straw house: The famous I'll huff and I'll puff line is from later retellings; Halliwell's early version has the wolf puffing and blowing the house in.
The Three Little Pigs, in story order.Straw house blown down: Straw is flimsy loose, but tightly packed straw bales, plastered over, make fire-resistant and well-insulated walls.
The Three Little Pigs, in story order.Wolf knocks at the stick house: In the earliest printed version the second house is made of furze, a prickly shrub, rather than sticks.
The Three Little Pigs, in story order.Stick house blown down: Disney's 1933 short Three Little Pigs gave the world Who's Afraid of the Big Bad Wolf?, a Depression-era hit.
The Three Little Pigs, in story order.Wolf huffs at the brick house: Fired brick has been made for over 4,000 years, which is why ancient brick buildings still stand.
The Three Little Pigs, in story order.Brick house stands firm: Bricks last: Roman fired-brick buildings and walls still stand across Europe, which explains the third pig's choice.
The Three Little Pigs, in story order.Wolf climbs onto the roof: In the story the wolf's climb sets up the final trick, while the pig plans for it with a pot of boiling water.
The Three Little Pigs, in story order.Wolf slides down the chimney: Chimneys in the era were wide enough for a person; in Britain boys were sent up them as chimney sweeps into the 19th century.
The Three Little Pigs, in story order.Wolf lands in the boiling pot: In Halliwell's version the pig cooks the wolf for supper, while modern retellings usually let the scalded wolf flee.

Abraham Lincoln's life, in order.Born in a log cabin: Lincoln was born in Kentucky and later moved to Indiana, and he had less than a year of formal schooling in total.
Abraham Lincoln's life, in order.Moves to Illinois: In Illinois Lincoln worked as a rail-splitter, store clerk and flatboat man before becoming a lawyer.
Abraham Lincoln's life, in order.Marries Mary Todd: Only one of Lincoln and Mary's four sons, Robert, survived to adulthood, and Mary struggled with the grief of the losses.
Abraham Lincoln's life, in order.Elected to Congress: Lincoln served one term in the US House and opposed the Mexican War, which cost him popularity at home.
Abraham Lincoln's life, in order.Debates Stephen Douglas: Lincoln lost the 1858 Senate race to Douglas, but the seven debates made him a national figure.
Abraham Lincoln's life, in order.Elected president: Lincoln was the first Republican elected president, winning in 1860 with only about 40 percent of the popular vote.
Abraham Lincoln's life, in order.Civil War begins: The Civil War began with the Confederate bombardment of Fort Sumter in South Carolina in April 1861.
Abraham Lincoln's life, in order.Gettysburg Address: The Gettysburg Address is only about 270 words long, and Lincoln spoke for around two minutes after a long main speech.
Abraham Lincoln's life, in order.Re-elected: Lincoln was the first president re-elected since Andrew Jackson in 1832, and he won with Andrew Johnson as running mate.
Abraham Lincoln's life, in order.Assassinated: John Wilkes Booth shot Lincoln at Ford's Theatre on April 14, 1865, and Lincoln died the next morning.

Emoji and emoticon milestones.Harvey Ball's smiley: Harvey Ball, a Massachusetts graphic artist, drew the yellow smiley for an insurance company in minutes and was paid $45.
Emoji and emoticon milestones.Fahlman's :-): Scott Fahlman proposed it on a Carnegie Mellon message board to mark jokes.
Emoji and emoticon milestones.Kurita's first emoji: Shigetaka Kurita designed 176 emoji of 12 by 12 pixels for NTT DoCoMo's mobile internet.
Emoji and emoticon milestones.Unicode adds emoji: Unicode standardised emoji so phones from different makers could exchange them.
Emoji and emoticon milestones.iPhone emoji keyboard: Apple's emoji keyboard arrived in iOS 5, whereas before it was available only in Japan.
Emoji and emoticon milestones.Emojipedia launches: Founded by Jeremy Burge, the site is a reference for what each emoji means.
Emoji and emoticon milestones.First World Emoji Day: It is held on July 17, the date shown on the calendar emoji on iOS.
Emoji and emoticon milestones.Skin tone emoji: Unicode added five modifiers based on the Fitzpatrick scale.
Emoji and emoticon milestones.MoMA acquires originals: The Museum of Modern Art acquired Kurita's original 176 emoji.
Emoji and emoticon milestones.The Emoji Movie: Sony's film about an emoji named Gene was widely panned and won a Razzie for worst picture.
